method: Option C hybrid — back-of-book index (calleja-index-raw.txt) augmented by Phase 2 concept-extractions from 13 deep JSONs

tier_definitions.1: Load-bearing volume-wide (appears in multiple units; structural to the argument)

lemmas.definition_paraphrastic: The sensory-affective register of gameplay; beauty as one mode of incorporation-quality. Not a formal aesthetic theory.
The player's capacity for intentional action in the game-world, conditioned by contingency; central Ch.4 macro-phase concept.
CALLEJA NEOLOGISM. The emergent narrative arising in/through play; the player's accumulated experiential trace as game-life-history, distinct from scripted-narrative.
Alterbiography modality where the player narrates the in-world life of a controlled entity (e.g., NPC, avatar) as a being.
Alterbiography modality where the player narrates the collective life of units controlled at miniature scale (strategy games).
Alterbiography modality where the player narrates their own avataric persona's history as autobiography.
Cognitive-perceptual focus mode; baseline pre-condition of any involvement dimension. Calleja cites attention-network neuroscience (Fan et al. 2002; Sturm+Willmes 2001) in Ch.2.
Player-controlled humanoid entity at scale-1 in the game-world; primary control-target distinct from miniatures.
Aesthetic register of game-world response: contemplative-affective.
The player's biological body as the locus of kinesthetic-controller engagement; conditions spatial involvement.
Internalized mental representation of game-world spatial structure; concept from Tolman (1948) and Lynch (1960). Equivalent to mental-maps cross-reference.
Spatial-temporal co-presence of multiple players within a shared virtual environment without necessary interaction.
Player-to-player coordination toward shared goals within shared involvement; one pole of the cohabitation-collaboration-competition triad.
Player-to-player adversarial coordination within shared involvement; co-pole with collaboration.
Malaby (2007) framework: unpredictable yet not-random outcome-conditions distinguishing games from other forms. Has performative, social, spatial sub-modes.
Sub-mode of contingency arising from player-skill execution variability.
Sub-mode of contingency arising from other-player unpredictability.
Sub-mode of contingency arising from spatial-environment variability.
Player's exertion of intentional input on game-entities; encompasses avatar-control, miniature-control, and the symbolic/symbiotic/mimetic subtypes.
Scale-1 humanoid-entity input; first-person or third-person follow.
Input modality where physical movement maps directly to in-world action (Wii-style gestural control).
Scale-N input where the player commands multiple small units (strategy games).
Input modality where player and avatar share a coupled action-perception loop in real-time.
Input modality where actions are mapped through arbitrary symbolic conventions (keyboard, controller buttons).
Index-equivalent of collaboration; cross-reference only.
Non-interactive scripted sequences embedded in gameplay; site of narrative-pull tension; Calleja cites Klevjer's defense.
1980s-90s cultural-imaginary backdrop to VR-promise rhetoric; Calleja frames Ch.2 against this trope.
Aarseth (1997) concept: text-machines requiring ergodic-non-trivial-effort traversal; foundational for treating games as a textual category.
Calleja's overarching umbrella-term for player-game relation; supersedes 'immersion'.
Brown+Cairns (2004) intermediate rung on the engagement-engrossment-total-immersion ladder.
Aarseth (1997) property of texts requiring non-trivial effort to traverse; loadbearing in Ch.7 narrative discussion.
Index-named involvement-modality keyed to ergodic-effort engagement.
Macro-phase of Ch.8 affective involvement; engagement-mode where game-world serves as alternative-experience site. Calleja cites Tuan 1998.
Media-psychology concept (Bryant+Davies, Grodal): players seek-out stimulus levels that maintain optimal arousal.
Macro-phase of Ch.5 spatial involvement; engagement-mode where the player learns the game-world topography.
Wittgensteinian method for treating games as related-by-overlapping-features rather than essence-defined; structural to Ch.1.
The constructed-imaginary status of game-content; engaged via Walton on make-believe.
Genettean narratological term for narrative point-of-view; Calleja extends to game-perspective.
The four conceptual challenges Calleja identifies in extant immersion/presence discourse; Ch.10 reviews their resolution via the incorporation framework.
Designer-discourse term Calleja treats with skepticism in Ch.9; resists positing fun as a foundational category.
Ermi+Mayra (2005) three-component model engaged in Ch.2 critique.
Calleja's tripartite framing: games can be analyzed as object, as process, as virtual environment.
Calleja's preferred frame: game-as-feedback-loop coupling player to system.
Calleja's family-resemblance approach to defining games; refuses essentialist definition.
Calleja's framing: games are hybrids of formal-rule-system + experiential-event + sociocultural-practice.
Formal-analytic frame: game treated as rule-artifact.
Experiential-analytic frame: game treated as enacted-event.
Calleja's preferred analytic frame for In-Game: games as inhabitable environments — anchors the incorporation thesis.
The social formations of co-players; conditions shared involvement.
Ch.9 ludic-involvement core concept; structures the goal-strategy-tactics-microtactics hierarchy.
Multi-level goal-structure model adopted from AI literature (Rosenbloom+Newell 1983) and goal-setting psychology (Locke+Latham 1990).
Multi-session player objectives at the apex of the goal hierarchy.
Smallest-scale moment-to-moment goal-level (e.g., dodge this attack); base of the goal hierarchy.
Designer-imposed goals tied to story-progression.
Player-set goals not encoded in the game-system.
Top-level game-encoded goals (win the match, complete the quest).
Intermediate-scale goals between microtactics and primary.
High-level plan-level of the goal hierarchy.
Game-internal nested goal-structures that function as games-within-games.
Game-system-encoded objectives distinguished from player-set personal goals.
Mid-scale action-plan level of the goal hierarchy.
The rule-enforcement apparatus of MMOGs, both designer-imposed and player-emergent.
Calleja's preferred metaphor for the incorporation-state; players inhabit game-worlds as one inhabits a place.
Single-locus Ch.2 reference to character-identification as a non-equivalent of immersion.
Lynch (1960) urban-design concept: the property of an environment that makes it cognitively mappable.
The faculty of mental projection; engaged in Ch.7 via Ryan-mediated Iser+Sartre; loadbearing for Ch.10 secondary-worlds discussion via Tolkien.
The conflated umbrella-term that Calleja's book argues against; subdivided into absorption-mode and transportation-mode by Calleja's analysis.
Sub-modality of immersion: concentration-attentional flavor.
Sub-modality of immersion: world-relocation flavor.
Salen+Zimmerman (2003) concept critiqued and partly retained by Calleja: the mistake of treating immersion as the goal of all game-design.

CALLEJA NEOLOGISM. The synthetic alternative to immersion/presence: a dual-direction relation in which the player incorporates the game-world (cognitively/affectively assimilates it) and the game-world incorporates the player (extends the player's effective domain).
Process by which player builds internal representation of game-world; central to Ch.5 spatial involvement.
Cross-text-reference relation; single-locus reference in Ch.7.
Calleja's umbrella replacement for immersion/presence/engagement; structurally divisible into 6 dimensions × 2 temporal phases.
PIM Dimension 5: emotion-in-gameplay; macro-phase = escapism + affect; cited via Grodal, Bryant+Davies.
Non-canonical involvement-modality named in index — ergodic-effort flavored engagement.
Calleja's comparative use of cinematic-engagement as foil; PIM is partly designed contra cinema-based immersion theory.
PIM Dimension 1: control + movement + agency.
Calleja's comparative use of literary-reading-engagement as foil; PIM partly designed contra Nell's lost-in-a-book reading-engagement.
PIM Dimension 6: rules + goals + choice + lusory-attitude.
PIM Dimension 4: scripted-narrative + alterbiography (emergent narrative).
PIM macro-phase: player's continued engagement after a play-session ends (rumination, social-discussion, anticipation of next session).
PIM macro-phase: player's anticipatory engagement before a play-session starts.
PIM Dimension 3: social co-presence + cohabitation + collaboration + competition.
PIM Dimension 2: virtual-environment habitation + exploration + navigation.
Local-area-network gaming as historic precursor to MMO social co-presence.
LARP referenced in Ch.9 magic-circle discussion as a borderline-case.
Bolter+Grusin (1999) concept engaged in Ch.2: the medium effacing itself to deliver content; Calleja qualifies its application to games.
Caillois (1962) term for rule-bound structured play; opposite of paidia.
Suits (1978) term for the player's voluntary acceptance of unnecessary obstacles to enable play.
PIM temporal-phase distinction: the off-line / between-sessions / dispositional-orientation toward the game. Co-pole with micro phase.
Huizinga (1955) concept of play as bounded act-apart; central foil in Ch.9 — Calleja qualifies the strong-circle reading via Pargman+Jakobsson, Malaby, Taylor.
Persistent-world multiplayer games central to Calleja's empirical case-base (WoW + Planetside).
Index cross-reference: see Cognitive maps.
PIM temporal-phase distinction: the moment-to-moment in-session engagement. Co-pole with macro phase.
Player-controlled small-scale entities (RTS units, strategy pieces); scale-N counterpart to scale-1 avatars.
Index cross-reference: see Control.
Ch.7 core concept; bifurcates into scripted-narrative (designer-encoded) and alterbiography (emergent).
Index cross-reference; index uses 'experiential' for alterbiography.
Walton (1990) make-believe-props concept: game-objects function as narrative props authorizing player imaginings.
Calleja's distinction: narrative-pull = the player drawing themselves toward narrative-revelation.
Calleja's distinction: narrative-push = the designer driving the story forward (via cutscenes etc.).
Designer-encoded story-content; bound at level of cutscenes, dialogue, mission-briefings.
Jenkins (2004) narrative-architecture concept: space carries narrative load.
The classical narrative-theory tradition Calleja engages (selectively) in Ch.7.
Caillois (1962) term for unstructured improvisational play; opposite of ludus.
CALLEJA'S CORE CONSTRUCT. The 6-dimensional × 2-phase model of player engagement: kinesthetic, spatial, shared, narrative, affective, ludic × macro/micro.
The presence-theory tradition Calleja contests; immersion's near-synonym in presence-research literature.
Waterworth+Waterworth (2003) framing — perceptual-illusion variant of presence-theory.
Ch.9 ludic-involvement co-concept: the goal-attainment reinforcement-feedback structure.
RPGs as a genre engaged for rule + narrative discussion.
Game-system constraints; Ch.9 distinguishes designer-encoded rules from socially-negotiated rules (Malaby, Taylor).
Player-emergent rule-modifications that complement formal game-rules.
Tolkien's sub-creation concept (Monsters and the Critics): inhabitable imaginative worlds; central to Ch.8 escapism analysis.
PIM Dimension 3 — the social-co-presence dimension; macro-phase = socializing in game-worlds.
The 6 PIM dimensions: kinesthetic, spatial, shared, narrative, affective, ludic.
Ch.5 core concept; distinguished into body-space, contingency-space, literary-space, navigated-space, socially-constructed-space, virtual-environment-habitation-space.
Sub-mode of spatial involvement: bodily-felt orientation in the game-world.
Sub-mode of spatial involvement: variable / unpredictable spatial conditions.
Sub-mode of spatial involvement comparative-reference to literary-fictional space.
Sub-mode of spatial involvement: route-following and wayfinding.
Lefebvre/Soja-derived framing of space as social-product.
PIM Dimension 2 — environment-habitation dimension; macro-phase = exploration.
Calleja's term for nested goal-structures functioning as games-within-games (e.g., crafting in MMOs).
Classical narrative-theory concept Calleja qualifies via the alterbiography apparatus.
Cross-modal sensory phenomenon invoked in Ch.10 to characterize incorporation's perceptual depth.
Sartrean imagination-as-synthesis concept; Ch.7 mediated via Ryan; Ch.10 invokes synthesizing-imagination of incorporation.
Index cross-reference.
Remote-operation prehistory of telepresence.
Minsky (1980) coinage; presence-theory's VR-engineering ancestor.
Adjacent VR-prehistory technology referenced in Ch.2.
Oldenburg (1999) concept appropriated for MMO sociality by Steinkuehler+Williams (2006); central in Ch.6.
Top rung of Brown+Cairns (2004) engagement-engrossment-total-immersion ladder.
Tuan (1974) affective-bond-with-place concept; partial scaffold for spatial+affective bridge.
Calleja's preferred ontological category for games; carrier of inhabitable / habitable affordance.
The full-relation phrase Calleja prefers: player-as-inhabitant-of-game-world. Direct synonym for the incorporation-state in the spatial register.
The technology-promise that Calleja's Ch.2 treats as immersion-discourse's cultural-driver and theoretical bog.
Player's route-discovery and environment-orientation behavior; Lynch (1960) urban-design term.
Klastrup-coined property of virtual-worlds' inhabitable-coherence; Calleja deploys in Ch.5.
Player-character identification noted as orthogonal to involvement.
Brown+Cairns (2004) progressive-immersion stage-model engaged as Ch.2 foil.
